title: Disaster Spreads from Samaria to Judah
overview: Micah announces that the LORD is coming to judge the capital cities of Israel and Judah, then mourns as he pictures the ruin reaching the towns around his own home.

parts.label: Who, when and about whom (v. 1)
parts.note: Micah came from Moresheth, a small town in the low hills southwest of Jerusalem, and spoke under three kings of Judah in the 700s BC. His message is aimed at Samaria and Jerusalem, the capitals of the northern kingdom (Israel) and the southern kingdom (Judah).

parts.label: The LORD comes as judge (vv. 2-4)
parts.note: The scene is like a courtroom, with the whole world called to listen as the LORD testifies against his people. Mountains melting like wax and valleys splitting open are poetic pictures of overwhelming power, drawn from earthquakes and fire.

parts.label: Samaria will be leveled (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: The capitals are named as the source of the nation's wrongdoing, especially worship of other gods at hilltop shrines, and Samaria is to become a field of rubble (it fell to Assyria around 722 BC). The shrines' riches are pictured as a prostitute's earnings, but the last line is unclear: perhaps conquerors will take that wealth for their own gods, or perhaps it will go back to Assyria, whose worship Israel had copied.

parts.label: The prophet grieves (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: Going barefoot and without an outer garment was a public sign of deep mourning, and Micah wails like a jackal or an ostrich crying at night. He grieves because the deadly 'wound' that ruined Samaria is spreading south, right up to Jerusalem's gate.

parts.label: Towns in mourning (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: 'Tell it not in Gath' echoes David's lament for King Saul and means: do not let enemies gloat. Each town's fate plays on its name; Beth Ophrah means 'house of dust,' Shaphir sounds like 'beauty,' and Maroth like 'bitterness.'

parts.label: Lachish to Adullam (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: The puns continue: Lachish sounds like 'team of horses' and Akzib like 'deception,' and Lachish is blamed as where Jerusalem's sin began, though why is unclear. Many scholars link these towns to the Assyrian invasion of 701 BC, and shaving the head was a mourning custom for children taken away into exile.

think: When trouble that once seemed far away reaches your own doorstep, how does that change the way you see it?
